## Voltage Tolerance and Ballast Logic in HID Systems

The core of your issue likely isn't a simple voltage drop from the battery or alternator, despite those being standard checks for low-light scenarios. Xenon HID systems operate on a fundamentally different logic than standard halogen bulbs. While you can measure system voltage at the battery terminals, that reading tells you nothing about the specific load conditions at the headlight assembly. The critical metric is the AC output of the ballast driving the bulb.

In a properly functioning HID circuit, the ballast acts as an inverter and regulator. It converts 12V DC into high-voltage AC (typically around 85 volts) to strike the arc, then regulates it down to roughly 32–34 volts AC to maintain the plasma discharge. If both headlights are dim simultaneously, the most probable culprit is a failure mode within one of the two ballasts. These units often degrade asymmetrically; one might be outputting full power while the other drops below its regulation threshold due to internal capacitor aging or coil saturation.

You mentioned checking if brightness depends on voltage. In this context, "voltage" usually refers to the input DC side. A healthy battery at 13.5V–14.5V under load will not prevent a failing ballast from collapsing its output regulation. The dimming is caused by the ballast unable to sustain the arc current required for full luminosity, regardless of what the alternator is putting out on the bus. To diagnose this without removing the bulbs immediately, you would need an oscilloscope or a multimeter capable of measuring RMS AC voltage at the connector behind the headlight lens while the engine is running. If one side reads significantly lower than 32V AC compared to the other (or if it fluctuates wildly), that ballast is dead and needs replacement.

## Bulb Lifespan and Arc Degradation

Regarding your second question: yes, xenon bulbs do get dimmer with age, but the mechanism is not thermal burnout in the traditional sense. Unlike incandescent filaments that thin out until they snap, HID arcs degrade through electrode erosion and phosphor coating breakdown on the bulb glass. Over 20,000 to 30,000 hours of operation, the electrodes shorten, increasing resistance and reducing arc efficiency. Simultaneously, the ceramic coating inside the bulb can yellow or flake, scattering light before it exits the lens.

This degradation is often gradual, making it easy to dismiss until you notice a sudden shift in brightness perception, which aligns with your observation that the issue appeared "fairly recently." However, if both bulbs are at the same mileage and showing identical symptoms, age alone explains the drop less effectively than simultaneous ballast failure. If one headlight were significantly dimmer than the other while driving on the highway, I would suspect bulb degradation first. Since they are matched in output but low compared to your wife's vehicle (which may have newer hardware or different calibration), the ballast regulation is the primary suspect.

## Optical Factors and Diagnostics

Before replacing parts, you must rule out optical attenuation. You noted cleaning the lenses resulted in transparency, which is good, but Xenon light exposes dirt accumulation differently than halogen light. The high-intensity UV component of an HID arc can degrade the polycarbonate plastic over years, causing micro-crystallization that looks clear to the naked eye but scatters light significantly. If your wife's car has newer lenses or a different model year with different material formulations, this could explain the brightness discrepancy even if both cars have dirty optics.

If you decide to swap components, order an aftermarket HID kit specifically designed for your 2002 Acura. These kits include a ballast and bulb set that often come with improved thermal management compared to OEM parts from that era. However, ensure the housing has adequate ventilation; forcing more power into a constrained space can lead to premature failure of new components.

Always cross-reference the ballast part number with your vehicle's VIN, as wiring harnesses vary between trim levels, which can cause confusion during installation.
